extracted.intended_audience: students, citizens, and practitioners interested in municipal government and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for organizing, staffing, budgeting, and supervising municipal governments; discusses forms (mayor-council, commission, city manager), departmental grouping, civil service, budgeting controls, and police administration. Intended to inform charter-makers, reformers, and students about features that make city government efficient, responsible, and democratically accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayoral appointing and removing power / responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate appointing and removing power in the mayor so he is responsible for the conduct of the whole administration and 'seeing that the laws and ordinances are faithfully executed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayor may appoint heads of major municipal departments and remove them (with some exceptions such as board of education members and judges). Where the mayor has large appointing/removing power he can make single-headed administration effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-headed administrative departments vs boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for single-headed administrative departments (one head appointed/removed by mayor) rather than board forms for efficiency and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-headed departments are widely regarded as desirable, but have defects: short terms and political reward status reduce efficiency; permanent tenure can create an official class that checks democratic control. Proposed compromise: unpaid policy boards with permanent technical officials chosen largely under civil service rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper grouping of departmental functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions should be grouped into departments according to city size and nature of duties so that responsibility is clear and administration efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation (as in commission government) groups allied functions under a few heads so each commissioner can be held responsible. Poor distribution (e.g., street cleaning under separate heads from pavement repair) causes conflict and 'pulling at cross purposes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Schaper departmental classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested model classification of municipal departments: I. City records; II. Law; III. Health and hospitals; IV. Public works; V. Finance; VI. Public safety; VII. Parks and public grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification is presented as suggestive for cities of considerable size; allied minor branches can be arranged under these leading departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special conference committee for interdepartmental coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee (mayor, city attorney, heads of four leading departments) to supervise general conduct of city's business including contracts, land acquisition, budget proposals, ordinance suggestions, and appointments under civil service rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed to unify work of departments and provide coordinated supervision across major functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit/civil service system — municipal commission
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipal civil service commission (appointed by mayor or governor) to oversee merit appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include municipal commissions in New York, Chicago, and Philadelphia; in some states cities are under a state commission appointed by the governor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit/civil service system — examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use examinations designed to test candidates' abilities for the several fields of city work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations form the competitive basis for appointment; the United States Civil Service Commission reported broad extension of the system in many cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit/civil service system — eligible list & mandatory selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointing officers should select subordinates from an 'eligible list' of candidates who passed required exams, often required to choose from top three or strictly the top candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some systems demand the appointing officer take the highest-ranked candidate and no other, to minimize patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit/civil service system — plan for removal
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear plan for removal of employees, either with or without a hearing on charges, as part of the civil service framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal procedures may vary; specifying removal rules is an element of the merit system to ensure accountability and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit/civil service system — pensioning employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish pension systems for certain municipal employees (e.g., teachers, policemen, firemen) as part of personnel policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pension systems are sometimes included to provide stability and career incentives in municipal service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of specialized civil servants with citizen experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use boards of citizen experts to cooperate with civil service commissions in examinations and selection for specialized posts (e.g., city engineer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kansas City example (1910): three engineers of high standing assisted the civil service commission to select an efficient city engineer — a model for selecting high-skill municipal employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative and referendum at municipal level
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt initiative and referendum so voters may initiate measures and force reference of ordinances, franchises, and other important municipal matters to the electorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least twenty states had adopted initiative and referendum for some or all cities; used to increase voter participation in municipal politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall of municipal officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide recall mechanisms allowing voters (by petition of a certain percentage) to force new elections for municipal officers perceived as dishonest or inefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used especially with commission government; Boston has a modified recall allowing the mayor to be recalled after two years. Iowa's scheme allows 25% of voters to petition for removal and forces a new election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of party conventions — nomination by petition or direct primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace party conventions with nomination by petition or direct primary to broaden participation and limit machine slates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston requires petitions signed by 5000 voters for mayor and council nominations; direct primary commonly used with commission form and non-partisan primaries reduce party machine control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission government — concentration of executive and legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission form vests full legislative and executive power in a small body (often five commissioners) elected at large, each assigned a department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: centralizes power and responsibility, coordinates taxing/spending, reduces maladjustments and barriers used by antisocial interests. Disadvantages: reduces deliberation and representation, excludes minority representation, may reduce civic ideals, and concentrates power that can be bought; recall and direct primaries are offered as remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: City manager plan (variation on commission government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission retains legislative/representative functions but appoints a city manager as chief executive with full power over executive business including appointment of subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim is to secure expert executive work while preserving representative commission; endorsed by the National Municipal League (circa 1913).

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget-making vested in a small responsible authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Take budget-making out of large councils and vest it in a smaller, more responsible body (e.g., board of estimate, mayor, comptroller) to improve control and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York's board of estimate and apportionment; Boston's mayor-originated budget with a governor-appointed finance commission for scrutiny; some councils may only reduce items, not increase totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public hearings and opportunity for stakeholders during budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide hearings so departments, taxpayers' associations, and interest groups (education, tenement inspection, transportation, etc.) can present claims during budget preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tentative estimates should be available well before final budget making; the public must be educated about budget importance to participate meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform bookkeeping and standardized departmental returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a uniform system of bookkeeping across departments and send uniform questions so estimates and costs mean the same thing across departments and divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay-rolls and maintenance estimates should be annual; when increases are requested, state whether for extra employees or higher salaries; technical uniformity aids meaningful comparison and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of tentative estimates and staged hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish tentative departmental estimates in advance and grant hearings while estimates are tentative and again after the final budget is ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also suggest publishing leading items of the tentative budget and explaining citizen demands that were rejected to increase transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict usage of appropriated moneys without authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a resolution with the budget that moneys appropriated may not be used for other purposes without authority from the appropriating body and without due notice to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to prevent officers from diverting funds to unintended uses and to ensure public notice of such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control pace of disbursements — divide payrolls across year
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide annual payroll allowances so monthly disbursements do not exceed one-twelfth of the total annual appropriation to prevent spending all funds early in the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents departmental 'bankruptcy' later in the fiscal year and encourages steadier financial management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern business methods, inspection and audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt modern business practices: describe work when done and money when spent, and maintain inspection and audit methods to ensure rules are complied with and 'the truth told.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary to make budget controls effective and to allow external authorities (comptroller, finance commission) to supervise expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public scrutiny and publicity in financial administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commissions of accounts, finance commissions, and public hearings to ensure scrutiny and publicity over appropriations, loans, and expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York's commissioners of accounts (limited success) and Boston's governor-appointed commission with investigative powers; publicity helps citizens and organizations influence budget priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal examples of procurement abuse underscore need for controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented cases (e.g., New York overpaying for coat hooks, nails, and street contracting abuses) illustrate how waste occurs without scientific bookkeeping and scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such examples as justification for uniform accounting, audits, commissions, and tighter contracting procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police administration — local versus state control
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize police as a branch of local government in most places, but consider state control or state-level supervision where local politics unduly influence enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: New York's metropolitan police under a state commission (later abolished), special state police divisions for election law enforcement, and police boards as branches of state administration in Baltimore, St. Louis, and Boston. State systems defend impartial enforcement against corrupt local influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed police coordination and oversight measures (Hatton's suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested plan to coordinate state and local police control including: police commissioners appointed by mayor with good-behavior term; removal by mayor after public statement of charges; removal of mayors/commissioners/sheriffs by governor after public statement for delinquency; a system of state inspection of local police; a small efficient state detective force; centralization of state inspection and detective work in a state bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures aim to combine local appointment with state oversight and investigatory support to protect impartial law enforcement and guard against local corrupt control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit important franchises and certain ordinances to popular vote (Iowa scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Iowa model, important franchises must be submitted to popular vote before taking effect; ordinances may be initiated by voters and some ordinances passed by commission must be referred on petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expands direct democratic control over major municipal decisions and acts as a check on concentrated administrative power.
